citation: Li et al., “Superconductivity in an infinite-layer nickelate,” Nature 572(7771), 624–627 (2019), DOI 10.1038/s41586-019-1496-5.
research_question: Topotactic reduction of epitaxial NdNiO3 and Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO3 precursor films to infinite-layer films and experimental superconductivity.
methods_and_model: 9–11 nm PLD films, CaH2 sealed-tube reduction at 260–280 C, XRD, transport, Hall, current-voltage, field dependence and mutual-inductance measurements.
main_findings: Reported Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 superconducting transition with onset 14.9 K, midpoint 13.6 K and zero resistance 9.1 K; sample-to-sample variation and indications of lateral reduction inhomogeneity are discussed.
limitations: Thin strained films; interface/polar discontinuity may contribute; no spatial map of superconductivity or reduction; no mechanism identified.
relationship_to_projects: Indirect motivation for spatial heterogeneity; contextual caution for single-orbital interface model because Hall response suggests multiband complexity and the paper discusses interface effects.
full_text_status: Full accepted manuscript and Methods read via DOE OSTI; Nature publisher record and PubMed also checked.
evidence_stance: Verified primary experimental precedent; motivates but does not establish either proposed model.

citation: Motoki Osada, Bai Yang Wang, Berit H. Goodge, Kyuho Lee, Hyeok Yoon, Keita Sakuma, Danfeng Li, Masashi Miura, Lena F. Kourkoutis, and Harold Y. Hwang, “A Superconducting Praseodymium Nickelate with Infinite Layer Structure,” Nano Letters 2020, 20(8), 5735–5740.
research_question: Can Pr-based infinite-layer nickelate films be synthesized, and does Sr-doped Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 superconduct? The authors also use Pr as a comparison with Nd to test whether superconductivity requires specific rare-earth 4f electronic effects, including direct 4f hybridization or Nd valence fluctuations.
methods_and_model: Experimental thin-film study, not a theoretical or tight-binding modeling paper. PrNiO3 and Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO3 precursor films were grown by pulsed-laser deposition on SrTiO3(001), then topotactically reduced with CaH2 to PrNiO2 and Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2. Characterization included X-ray diffraction and reciprocal-space mapping, cross-sectional STEM/EELS, four-probe resistivity, patterned-device current–voltage measurements, and two-coil mutual-inductance measurements. The authors examined five doped films 5.3–12 nm thick, including one with a 2 nm SrTiO3 cap.
main_findings: The paper reports successful synthesis of infinite-layer PrNiO2 and Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 films. The doped films show a superconducting transition with onset Tc=12 K and zero-resistance Tc=7 K, and a critical current density of 334 kA/cm² at 2 K. Mutual-inductance data show a diamagnetic screening response below the zero-resistance transition, interpreted as global superconductivity; the inferred London penetration depth is on the micron scale. The undoped PrNiO2 film has a low-temperature resistivity upturn. The authors argue that comparable superconductivity in Pr- and Nd-based films makes finely tuned rare-earth 4f hybridization and Nd-specific valence fluctuations unnecessary, while the role of 4f magnetism remains unknown.
limitations: This is a thin-film materials synthesis and characterization report centered on one Sr concentration (x=0.2), not a comprehensive Pr phase diagram or a microscopic mechanism study. The authors state they had not yet performed an equally extensive optimization study for Pr films and explicitly say the role of 4f magnetism is unknown. Across the five films tested, Tc and normal-state resistivity did not vary systematically with thickness, but normal-state resistivity showed sample-to-sample variability attributed by the authors to extended defects. The evidence supports superconductivity in the measured films but does not identify its pairing mechanism or establish that every infinite-layer nickelate shares identical behavior.
relationship_to_projects: Spatial percolation manuscript: relevant experimental context for superconducting Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 films, film thicknesses, extended-defect variability, and the need to distinguish zero resistance from bulk/global screening. It does not model spatial inhomogeneity, connectivity, percolation thresholds, or local superconducting domains, so it is not direct validation of a percolation model. One-orbital interface tight-binding notebook: relevant as a material/platform reference for epitaxial Pr-based infinite-layer films on SrTiO3, square-planar NiO2 structure, strain, and an observed superconducting state. It does not provide an interface tight-binding Hamiltonian, orbital-resolved bands, fitted hopping parameters, or a one-orbital justification; any mapping to that notebook would require independent theoretical or spectroscopic support.
full_text_status: The 19-page primary manuscript is accessible as the arXiv PDF (arXiv:2006.13369). The ACS page and PubMed record were readable for metadata/abstract; the ACS full article was not accessible in this session. No supplement file was located in the consulted ACS Figshare search or publisher-page extraction, so supplement availability and contents remain unconfirmed.
evidence_stance: Verified as an exact journal paper. Publisher and PubMed records confirm title, ordered authors, Nano Letters volume/issue/pages, 2020 publication, and DOI; arXiv links the manuscript to that DOI. The full accessible primary manuscript supports the described synthesis, measurement methods, results, operational definitions, and stated caveats. Treat the proposed insensitivity to rare-earth 4f details as the authors’ interpretation from a Pr–Nd comparison, not as proof of mechanism. Supplementary-information status is unresolved, not evidence that no supplement exists.

citation: Shengwei Zeng, Changjian Li, Lin Er Chow, Yu Cao, Zhaoting Zhang, Chi Sin Tang, Xinmao Yin, Zhi Shiuh Lim, Junxiong Hu, Ping Yang, and Ariando Ariando, ‘Superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelate La1−xCaxNiO2 thin films,’ Science Advances 8(7), eabl9927 (published 18 February 2022).
research_question: Whether Ca substitution in infinite-layer La1−xCaxNiO2 thin films can produce superconductivity, and how the superconducting phase diagram and normal-state transport (particularly the Hall coefficient) evolve with Ca content, in relation to the electronic and lattice behavior of other infinite-layer nickelates.
methods_and_model: The authors made nominal La1−xCaxNiO3 perovskite precursor films by pulsed-laser deposition on TiO2-terminated (001) SrTiO3, then used CaH2 topotactic reduction to obtain the infinite-layer films. They characterized structure using synchrotron X-ray diffraction and cross-sectional HAADF-STEM, and measured resistivity and Hall transport in a physical-property measurement system. For x=0.23, field suppression of superconductivity was analyzed by fitting upper-critical-field versus midpoint-transition data with a Ginzburg–Landau model. The study is an experimental film/transport investigation, not a microscopic tight-binding or spatial-percolation model.
main_findings: The reported phase diagram has a superconducting dome over approximately 0.15 < x < 0.3. Undoped and underdoped samples through x≤0.15 are insulating from 300 K down to 2 K; the overdoped x≥0.3 samples show increased normal-state resistivity and weakly insulating low-temperature behavior. For higher doping, the Hall coefficient changes sign on cooling in most reported samples at x≥0.23 (the paper notes an exception at x=0.25); the sign-change temperature is around 35 K and does not appreciably shift with doping in that regime. A representative x=0.23 film was reported as 17 nm thick and showed an infinite-layer structure by STEM. The authors interpret the data as evidence that lattice environment/dopant identity and multiband structure matter, while treating the detailed mechanism as unresolved.
limitations: The article does not provide a dedicated limitations section. Its evidence is from Ca-doped LaNiO2 thin films over the tested composition range, and the reported results do not by themselves establish a microscopic pairing mechanism or spatially resolved superconducting connectivity. The authors explicitly call for further theoretical and experimental work to clarify the role of 4f orbitals in the (multi)band nature of nickelates and the distinctive Hall-sign-change behavior. The supplementary PDF is available by link in the article record but was inaccessible during this verification, so supplementary-only details were not checked.
relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, the paper is useful as an experimental benchmark for a doping-dependent superconducting dome and insulating transport regimes in an infinite-layer nickelate, but it does not measure spatial superconducting patches, connectivity, or a percolation threshold; it cannot directly validate a percolation model. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it offers qualitative empirical context for doping-dependent transport and the influence of lattice environment, but it contains no interface-specific tight-binding calculation and no one-orbital model. Its discussion of multiband structure and lattice/dopant effects is a caution against presenting a one-orbital model as a complete description of this material without independent justification.
full_text_status: The publisher’s DOI record and the complete primary article text in PubMed Central were accessible and inspected; this was not an abstract-only verification. The article links Supplementary Materials comprising Figs. S1–S6, but attempts to retrieve the PDF were blocked by a PMC browser-verification/reCAPTCHA page, so the supplement itself was not inspected.
evidence_stance: Verified as an exact published article, not merely a close title match: the publisher DOI page confirms the title, journal, date, volume/issue, and DOI; the PMC primary article provides the complete author list, article number, methods, results, and discussion; PubMed and arXiv independently cross-check the metadata. The supplied citation fields are correct. Supplementary materials are advertised but were not independently examined, and no conclusions here rely on their unseen contents.

citation: A. S. Botana and M. R. Norman, "Similarities and Differences between LaNiO2 and CaCuO2 and Implications for Superconductivity," Physical Review X 10, 011024 (2020).
research_question: What electronic-structure and magnetic similarities and differences distinguish infinite-layer RNiO2 (R = La, Nd) from the cuprate CaCuO2, and what do those comparisons imply for nickelate superconductivity? The authors focus on hopping amplitudes, orbital energy splittings, charge-transfer energy, spacer-cation states, magnetism, and the evolution under Sr doping.
methods_and_model: First-principles calculations used the all-electron WIEN2k APW+lo method. Nonmagnetic calculations used PBE-GGA; Ni correlations were also examined with LDA+U in fully localized limit and around-mean-field schemes (U_Ni = 1.4–6 eV, J = 0.8 eV). They compared LaNiO2 with CaCuO2 and noted that NdNiO2's band structure is nearly identical to LaNiO2's for their purpose. Maximally localized Wannier functions and Slater-Koster fits supplied orbital and hopping parameters. A six-parameter single-band tight-binding fit described the Fermi-level d_x2-y2 antibonding band. Magnetic configurations and Sr-doped supercells were also studied; Hall coefficients were calculated from the band structure. Lattice parameters, k-point mesh, convergence settings, and supercell sizes are specified in the manuscript.
main_findings: The calculated one-band fits give t′/t = 0.37 for both LaNiO2 and CaCuO2, with nickelate nearest-neighbor hopping magnitude about 80% of the cuprate value. Wannier-derived d-p charge-transfer energy is substantially larger for LaNiO2 (4.4 eV) than CaCuO2 (2.7 eV), while the Wannier eg splitting is comparable (0.7 versus 1.0 eV). Rare-earth 5d electron pockets near the Fermi level self-dope the nickelate's large hole-like d_x2-y2 Fermi surface; the calculations find that Sr doping suppresses rare-earth-derived states and makes the electronic structure more single-band/cuprate-like. GGA spin-polarized calculations find a C-type antiferromagnetic solution for LaNiO2, but the paper notes the lack of experimental evidence for antiferromagnetic order. The authors conclude that several cuprate-associated electronic parameters are favorable, while the larger charge-transfer energy and rare-earth pockets remain important differences; these are electronic-structure implications, not a demonstrated superconducting mechanism.
limitations: This is a computational comparative electronic-structure study, not a direct experimental test of superconductivity or a derivation of a superconducting order parameter. Results depend on the chosen DFT and LDA+U treatments, crystal structures, Wannier projections, and fitting assumptions. The rigid-band doping estimate is an approximation; the paper separately uses finite Sr-doped supercells. LaNiO2 is emphasized to avoid complications from Nd 4f states, so detailed Nd-specific f-electron physics is outside the central comparison. The authors report that their magnetic calculations yield C-type AFM even though experimental AFM order was not established, highlighting uncertainty in interpreting that prediction. The manuscript has no dedicated limitations section. The supplemental file's detailed results were not available for independent inspection in this verification.
relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, this paper is contextual materials/electronic-structure background only. It does not formulate spatial percolation, connectivity thresholds, disorder-driven cluster formation, or transport through percolating paths, so it is not evidence for a percolation claim. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it is more directly useful as a parameterization reference: it provides a d_x2-y2-derived single-band fit and reports t′/t = 0.37 for both comparison materials, alongside multiorbital Wannier parameters. However, it does not model interfaces or spatially varying interface hoppings, and its fitted parameters should not be assumed to apply to the notebook's interface geometry without separate justification. Its multiorbital comparison also cautions that reducing the nickelate to one orbital leaves out rare-earth pockets and the larger d-p splitting.
full_text_status: The APS publisher record and DOI were consulted, and a complete readable arXiv manuscript (v3, arXiv:1908.10946) was accessible. APS lists supplemental material covering band structures, Fermi surfaces, Wannier functions, Slater-Koster fits, Hall calculations, and magnetic band structures. The supplement landing/description was inspected, but the supplemental file itself could not be retrieved because APS access returned a Cloudflare challenge; supplement-specific findings therefore are not claimed here.
evidence_stance: The candidate is verified as an exact published citation: title, authors, journal, volume/article number, publication year, and DOI agree across the APS DOI/publisher record and independent institutional/arXiv records. The accessible arXiv v3 provides full-paper evidence for the reported methods and findings. The APS supplement is confirmed to exist and its declared scope is known, but the supplemental file itself was not inspected; no supplement-only claim is used.

citation: Yusuke Nomura, Motoaki Hirayama, Terumasa Tadano, Yoshihide Yoshimoto, Kazuma Nakamura, and Ryotaro Arita, “Formation of a two-dimensional single-component correlated electron system and band engineering in the nickelate superconductor NdNiO2,” Physical Review B 100, 205138 (2019), published 26 November 2019.
research_question: The paper asks how Nd-layer states affect the correlated Ni 3d(x2−y2) electrons in parent infinite-layer NdNiO2: what minimal low-energy orbital model captures the Fermi pockets; how strongly Ni and Nd-layer bands hybridize; whether metallic screening from the Nd layer weakens the Ni Hubbard interaction enough to matter for phonon-mediated superconductivity; and whether band engineering can suppress the extra Nd-layer pockets to approach a single-component Mott-Hubbard system.
methods_and_model: First-principles electronic structures were calculated with PBE density-functional theory (Quantum ESPRESSO; an xTAPP comparison was also used) and fitted with maximally localized Wannier functions using RESPACK. The minimal model retains Ni 3d(x2−y2), Nd 5d(3z2−r2), and an interstitial-s-centered orbital that bonds with Nd 5dxy. cRPA was used to estimate screened Coulomb parameters for three-orbital and single-orbital subspaces. Phonons and electron-phonon coupling were calculated using density-functional perturbation theory and assessed with the Allen-Dynes formula. For proposed band-engineered compounds, the authors used structural optimization and DFT band calculations. The article also compares an alternative three-orbital representation using Nd 5dxy, and its appendices analyze screening and that alternative model.
main_findings: The three-orbital Wannier model reproduces the near-Fermi-level bands; Ni-Nd-layer hybridization is reported as very small, and the Ni 3d(x2−y2) band is highly two-dimensional. The Nd-derived pockets occur around Γ and A, and their finite occupation leaves the Ni orbital at about 0.87 filling in the calculation. In cRPA, the Ni onsite U is about 3.1 eV in the three-orbital model and about 2.6 eV in the single-orbital model including Nd-layer screening, a reduction below 20%; the single-band nearest hopping is about −0.37 eV, giving |U/t| about 7. The calculated electron-phonon coupling is lambda=0.22 at the listed 0.04-Ry smearing and remains below 0.5 for the reported reasonable smearing widths; Allen-Dynes estimates are far below the experimental 9–15 K range, so the paper rules out phonons as the exclusive explanation, not all possible superconducting mechanisms. The authors predict that reducing interstitial-s–cation-dxy hybridization shrinks the extra pockets; these nearly disappear in calculated NaNd2NiO4 and NaCa2NiO3 band structures.
limitations: The paper is a first-principles/modeling study, not a spatial-disorder or percolation analysis, and it does not calculate a superconducting pairing state or establish the mechanism of the observed superconductivity. Its phonon result tests the conventional electron-phonon channel as an exclusive explanation under the stated calculation and Allen-Dynes assumptions. The effective interactions depend on the Wannier subspace and cRPA screening partition. Nd 4f electrons are frozen in core for the stated calculations. NaNd2NiO4 and NaCa2NiO3 are proposed computational candidates; their predicted band structures do not by themselves establish experimental synthesis or superconductivity. These are limitations of scope/modeling evident from the manuscript, not a list explicitly labeled by the authors as a formal limitations section.
relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, this is background on bulk NdNiO2's multiband electronic structure and screening, not evidence for geometric percolation, spatial connectivity, disorder-driven transitions, or percolation thresholds; do not cite it as support for those results. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it provides a useful bulk Ni 3d(x2−y2) reference and one set of hopping/interacting-model parameters, and supports treating Ni-derived states as weakly coupled to Nd-layer bands in this specific bulk calculation. It is not an interface Hamiltonian: it does not derive interface potentials, interfacial hopping, altered coordination, disorder, or layer-dependent parameters. Its single-orbital reduction is a controlled low-energy representation alongside additional Nd-derived pockets, not proof that every interface system is intrinsically single-band.
full_text_status: Publisher record and abstract verified; APS full article itself required credentials. The complete arXiv v2 manuscript (arXiv:1909.03942, 28 November 2019) was accessible and inspected, including its appendices A and B. No separate supplemental file was located through the APS supplemental endpoint or the arXiv record; the accessible appendices are part of the manuscript. Thus the scientific summary is based on the accessible full preprint, not a full-text inspection of the publisher-formatted version.
evidence_stance: Exact candidate exists and the supplied authors, publication year, venue, article number, and DOI are confirmed. The APS publisher metadata and Crossref record establish the published citation; arXiv supplies the accessible full manuscript. Bibliographic verification is high confidence. Technical claims are attributed to the arXiv v2 manuscript and are theoretical calculations/predictions rather than independent experimental verification. APS full text was not accessible without credentials, and no separate supplement was found.

citation: K.-W. Lee and W. E. Pickett, “Infinite-layer LaNiO₂: Ni¹⁺ is not Cu²⁺,” Physical Review B 70, 165109 (2004).
research_question: The paper asks why formally d⁹ infinite-layer LaNiO₂, with nominal Ni¹⁺, behaves differently from isostructural CaCuO₂ with Cu²⁺, especially in its metallicity, magnetic behavior, oxygen–transition-metal covalency, and possible role of electronic correlations.
methods_and_model: First-principles electronic-structure calculations used the full-potential nonorthogonal local-orbital (FPLO) method. The authors examined paramagnetic LDA bands and densities of states, attempted ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic solutions, and applied two common LDA+U functional forms over U = 1–8 eV while fixing intra-atomic exchange J = 1 eV. The AFM calculations used a √2 × √2 supercell; the Brillouin-zone mesh contained 196 k points in the irreducible wedge. Results were compared with CaCuO₂. The authors also fitted the Ni 3d(x²−y²)-derived band with a single-band tight-binding dispersion.
main_findings: The authors attribute LaNiO₂’s differences from CaCuO₂ mainly to weaker Ni 3d–O 2p mixing, associated with a larger separation of their site energies (at least 2 eV greater than the cuprate comparison), and to low-lying La 5d states mixing with Ni 3d(3z²−r²). The latter produces an additional Fermi-surface pocket and hole-dopes the Ni-derived bands; the calculated Fermi surface is not a single-band surface. LDA yields a weak AFM solution with 0.53 μB per Ni, 6 meV/Ni below the paramagnetic state, despite the cited absence of observed long-range magnetic order. In LDA+U the moment peaks near 0.8 μB at U = 3 eV and declines at larger U; at U = 8 eV, opposing polarization of the x²−y² and 3z²−r² orbitals nearly cancels the net moment. The authors explicitly characterize this large-U state as outside the plausible physical range for LaNiO₂ and not an explanation of its observed behavior.
limitations: The work is a band-theory study of the majority infinite-layer phase, not a treatment of the minority disordered phase, synthesis stability, or energetics; the authors explicitly say they do not address stability energetics. Its LDA AFM prediction conflicts with the experimental lack of observed long-range order, and the authors suggest magnetic fluctuations may correct LDA’s magnetic tendency, but do not calculate those fluctuations. The unusual large-U state is explicitly beyond the plausible U range and is sensitive to multiple LDA+U solutions; the paper notes a different U = 8 eV result in earlier work and says the reason for the discrepancy was unknown. The single-band fit does not represent the additional La/Ni-derived Fermi-surface pockets or all orbital mixing.
relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, this is background on LaNiO₂ band structure and orbital hybridization only. It does not formulate spatial percolation, disorder thresholds, connectivity, or percolative transport, so it should not be cited as direct evidence for those mechanisms. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, it is directly useful as a bulk-material reference: it provides an explicit Ni x²−y² single-band fit and motivates retaining orbital-mixing caveats. However, its calculated La 5d/Ni 3z²−r² and other pockets, plus reported kz dispersion, show that a one-orbital reduction is an approximation; the paper supplies no interface-specific hopping or boundary parameters. Its bulk fit parameters should not be transferred to an interface without independent justification.
full_text_status: The APS publisher record and abstract were accessible, but the article body was behind an authorization prompt. The complete 7-page arXiv v1 manuscript (with 8 figures) was accessible and inspected at https://arxiv.org/pdf/cond-mat/0405570. No supplement was listed on the APS record or arXiv record consulted; none was found.
evidence_stance: Verified with high confidence: the APS publisher record and independent Crossref metadata agree on the paper’s authorship, Physical Review B volume 70, article 165109, 2004 publication, and DOI; the accessible arXiv manuscript confirms the study’s content. Findings above distinguish the paper’s calculated results from its cited experimental context and explicitly preserve its caveats. The publisher’s full article text was not accessible in this session, but the full arXiv manuscript was.

citation: A. Ohtomo and H. Y. Hwang, ‘A high-mobility electron gas at the LaAlO3/SrTiO3 heterointerface,’ Nature 427(6973), 423–426 (2004), published 29 January 2004.
research_question: Whether an atomically controlled LaAlO3/SrTiO3 perovskite-oxide heterointerface, whose two possible terminations have different polarity, can host different interfacial charge states and transport behavior. The abstract frames the inquiry as a model of polarity discontinuity at an oxide interface.
methods_and_model: The abstract says the authors examined insulating LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 and controlled interface termination at the atomic scale. The publisher’s visible captions identify (001)-oriented interface schematics and transport comparisons for the (LaO)+/(TiO2)0 interface grown at oxygen partial pressures of 10^-4, 10^-5, and 10^-6 torr, plus a 10^-6-torr-grown sample annealed in 1 atm O2 at 400 °C for 2 h. Another caption identifies low-temperature magnetoresistance for a 60-Å LaAlO3 layer grown at 10^-6 torr. These visible materials support that growth conditions and transport were compared; they do not expose the full deposition, sample-preparation, instrumentation, or data-analysis protocol.
main_findings: According to the abstract, the simple ionic picture assigns an extra half electron or half hole per two-dimensional unit cell depending on interface structure. The hole-doped interface was insulating; the electron-doped interface was conducting, with carrier mobility exceeding 10,000 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. The authors report low-temperature magnetoresistance oscillations periodic in inverse magnetic field and interpret them as indicating quantum transport. The visible figure captions also identify transport and Hall-related comparisons, but the full data and analysis were not accessible here.
limitations: The full paper and any supplement could not be inspected, so experimental details, uncertainty estimates, alternative mechanisms, and the authors’ full qualifications cannot be assessed from the accessible sources. The Nature corrigendum states that Fig. 2a,b y-axis labels should be ohms per square, not milliohms per square, and says this error did not alter the results or conclusions. The caption-visible oxygen-pressure and annealing conditions do not, by themselves, establish a mechanism for conductivity.
relationship_to_projects: For the spatial percolation manuscript, this is relevant experimental context for termination-dependent conductivity at an LAO/STO interface and for polar charge asymmetry. The accessible record does not report spatially resolved conducting paths, percolation, or a percolation threshold, so it should not be cited as direct experimental evidence for those claims. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, the paper provides a qualitative polar-charge-counting and conducting-versus-insulating benchmark. It does not specify a one-orbital tight-binding model, hopping parameters, band structure, or orbital-resolved evidence, so it cannot validate those model choices directly.
full_text_status: Publisher record and abstract are accessible, along with figure captions and bibliographic metadata. The article body and PDF are subscription-gated; the publisher PDF endpoint returned the same preview. The ResearchGate record says no full text is available and offers a request rather than a manuscript. No accessible accepted manuscript or supplementary information was located or inspected. Therefore, methods and conclusions below are limited to the abstract, visible captions, and corrigendum, not a full-text reading.
evidence_stance: The candidate paper’s existence and citation are confirmed independently by the Nature publisher record and PubMed. The title, authors, venue, year, volume, pages, and DOI all match the candidate. Confidence in bibliographic verification is high; scientific-content verification is necessarily limited because only the abstract, visible figure captions, and correction were accessible, not the complete primary paper or an accepted manuscript.

citation: Satoshi Okamoto and Andrew J. Millis, “Electronic reconstruction at an interface between a Mott insulator and a band insulator,” Nature 428, 630–633 (2004), published 8 April 2004.
research_question: The paper asks how the electronic phase near an interface between a strongly correlated Mott insulator and a band insulator differs from the phases in the bulk. The authors frame this interfacial change as electronic reconstruction. The accessible publisher abstract characterizes the work as theoretical.
methods_and_model: For the exact Nature paper, the publisher’s Figure 1 caption identifies a ground-state phase diagram computed in Hartree–Fock as a function of on-site Coulomb interaction U and inverse La-layer number n; its other captions describe spin- and orbital-resolved charge profiles, total and metallic-subband charge profiles, and Fermi-surface contours. The accessible abstract and captions do not provide the complete methodological specification. As contextual—not exact-paper—detail, the accessible author-hosted companion study by Okamoto and Millis, “Theory of Mott insulator–band insulator heterostructures” (Phys. Rev. B 70, 075101), specifies a LaTiO3/SrTiO3 heterostructure with three Ti t2g orbitals, nearest-neighbor tight-binding bands, electrostatic fields treated in Hartree approximation, and on-site interactions treated in unrestricted Hartree–Fock. Do not cite those implementation details as directly inspected text of the Nature article.
main_findings: The Nature abstract reports that over wide parameter ranges the near-interface region is metallic and ferromagnetic, while the bulk on either side is insulating and antiferromagnetic. Publisher captions show that the paper presents a Hartree–Fock ground-state phase diagram, layer-resolved spin/orbital charge densities, charge in metallic subbands, and in-plane Fermi-surface contours. In the distinct companion PRB paper, the authors report that the outer roughly three layers are generally metallic, with a bulk-like central region for LaTiO3 blocks of six or more layers; this is corroborating context from that companion, not a verbatim claim verified from the Nature full text.
limitations: The main text of the exact Nature letter was not accessible, so detailed equations, parameter values, convergence procedures, and any qualifications or caveats in the body cannot be independently checked from that article here. The findings are theoretical and, from the accessible abstract, apply across wide model-parameter ranges; they should not be read as experimental confirmation for every interface. The authors’ accessible companion paper itself notes idealizations, including neglected small structural distortions and a simplified dielectric treatment; those details belong to the companion study. The full Nature supplementary-material status could not be established beyond finding no supplement link on the inspected publisher page.
relationship_to_projects: Spatial percolation manuscript: relevant as a theoretical precedent for interface-localized redistribution and metallic layers, with spatially varying charge and magnetic/orbital character. It is not a spatial-percolation study: the publisher material describes layered heterostructures and Hartree–Fock profiles, not quenched disorder, connected-cluster statistics, or a percolation threshold. One-orbital interface tight-binding notebook: useful as a qualitative motivation or contrast for a simplified one-orbital interface model, since the publisher confirms layer-dependent electronic reconstruction and the companion theory supplies a microscopic tight-binding/Hartree–Fock framework. It is not a direct parameter-level validation of a one-orbital notebook: the accessible companion model uses three Ti t2g orbitals, long-range electrostatics, and multi-orbital interactions. The exact Nature text is not fully accessible, so do not overclaim that every companion-model detail appears in the Nature letter.
full_text_status: The exact Nature article is verified from its publisher page and PubMed record, and the publisher abstract and figure captions are accessible. The full article text was not accessible: Nature displays subscription access, and ResearchGate says no full text is available there and offers only a request-to-author option. No accepted manuscript for this exact Nature article was found in the sources checked. No supplementary-information link was visible on the publisher page inspected. An author-hosted full-text companion paper by the same authors is accessible, but it is a different publication (Phys. Rev. B 70, 075101; DOI 10.1103/PhysRevB.70.075101), not the target article.
evidence_stance: Verified exact existence and bibliographic identity with high confidence: the Nature publisher page and PubMed agree on title, authors, year, volume, pages, and DOI; the publisher additionally gives the publication date. Substantive claims about the target paper are limited to its accessible abstract and figure captions. Detailed model specifications are identified explicitly as coming from the authors’ separate, accessible 2004 companion PRB paper. No unsupported equation, supplement, or exact-paper full-text claim is inferred.

citation: Massimiliano Stengel and David Vanderbilt, “Berry-phase theory of polar discontinuities at oxide-oxide interfaces,” Physical Review B 80, 241103(R) (2009), published 8 December 2009. DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.80.241103.
research_question: How should the polar discontinuity and interface charge at a coherent, insulating, charge-mismatched oxide interface be reconciled with the electrostatic boundary condition that the normal component of electric displacement D is continuous? The paper asks whether the usual boundary law can be retained microscopically without introducing a separate compositional-charge term.
methods_and_model: The authors derive the result using the modern Berry-phase theory of polarization and the interface theorem, defining formal polarization from ionic-core charges and Wannier centers. They also define planar/macroscopically averaged local polarization and displacement. As a first-principles illustration they calculate a periodic tetragonal (LaAlO3)4/(SrTiO3)4, 1×1 superlattice using LDA density-functional theory and PAW, a 60-Ry plane-wave cutoff, a 6×6×1 k-point grid, and relaxed ionic positions and out-of-plane stress. They compare Wannier-based local formal polarization with a Born-effective-charge/displacement estimate of effective polarization, and compare the interior layer relaxations with bulk LAO and STO calculated at the superlattice's constrained D.
main_findings: For the stated coherent insulating interface, the longitudinal component of D is continuous when P is the formal, branch-valued polarization of the modern theory. The interface bound charge equals the discontinuity in the formal bulk polarizations; the apparent conflict with D continuity arises from treating the polar discontinuity as if it were outside that formal polarization accounting. In the LAO/STO example, the formal local polarization is nearly uniform around the supercell average (reported as −0.365 C/m²), while the effective local polarization pattern has an abrupt jump; the LAO and STO structural distortions point oppositely. Interior layer bucklings agree with constrained-D bulk values to within about 3 mÅ. The relaxed superlattice remains insulating, with a reported gap of about 1.5 eV.
limitations: The theoretical boundary result is scoped to coherent insulating interfaces and the stated periodicity/neutrality construction; it is not a treatment of conducting interfaces, free-carrier screening, disordered or nonperiodic percolation networks, or arbitrary reconstruction. The worked calculation is a specific idealized 1×1 tetragonal LAO/STO superlattice within LDA, not a general empirical test across oxide interfaces. Polarization is branch-valued and local-cell assignments depend on basis/grouping, so formal and effective local polarization should not be conflated. The paper itself flags that nonperiodic in-plane situations, such as randomly distributed δ-doping, may call for compositional-charge treatment instead. No separate supplement was found/listed in the publisher or arXiv records inspected.
relationship_to_projects: Spatial percolation manuscript: relevant as conceptual electrostatic background for how formal polarization discontinuities and normal-D boundary conditions operate across ideal insulating interfaces. It does not derive percolation connectivity, thresholds, cluster statistics, or electrostatics in a spatially disordered/percolating medium, so it cannot by itself validate those manuscript claims. One-orbital interface tight-binding notebook: relevant as motivation for an interface charge/boundary-potential convention and for distinguishing formal interface charge from mobile carriers. The Berry-phase formal polarization and ionic/Wannier charge bookkeeping are not automatically represented by a one-orbital Hamiltonian; a notebook would need explicit background/interface charge and an electrostatic boundary prescription to model analogous effects. The paper does not provide or validate that tight-binding model.
full_text_status: The APS publisher page confirms the citation and exposes the abstract, but its article body is subscription-restricted. The complete four-page primary-paper manuscript (arXiv v1, with HTML/PDF) was accessible and read at arXiv/ar5iv. No separate supplement was listed on the APS or arXiv pages inspected.
evidence_stance: Verified. The exact title, both authors, Physical Review B volume/article number and Rapid Communication marker, publication year/date, and DOI agree between the APS publisher record and Crossref; the arXiv record independently links the same journal reference and DOI. Scientific claims above were checked against the accessible full primary-paper manuscript, not inferred from the abstract alone. Relevance statements are limited to conceptual overlap with the named project themes, which were not themselves supplied for review.

citation: Abel Weinrib and B. I. Halperin, “Critical phenomena in systems with long-range-correlated quenched disorder,” Physical Review B 27(1), 413–427 (1983).
research_question: How does quenched disorder whose spatial correlations decay as a power law affect critical-point stability and scaling, and how should the Harris criterion be extended? The abstract says the question is treated for an m-vector model and also applied to percolation with long-range-correlated site- or bond-occupation probabilities.
methods_and_model: The abstract describes a spatially varying local transition temperature with disorder correlation decaying as a power law at large separation, an m-vector model analyzed by a renormalization-group expansion in ε=4−d and δ=4−a, and an extension to percolation with long-range-correlated occupation probabilities. It also reports comparison with percolation properties of the triangular Ising model. Full-text details of the derivations and analysis could not be checked.
main_findings: The abstract reports an extended Harris criterion: for a<d, disorder is irrelevant when aν−2>0; for a>d, the usual condition dν−2=−α>0 is recovered. It reports a new long-range-disorder fixed point alongside the previously known short-range-disorder and pure fixed points, crossover consistent with the extended criterion, complex eigenvalues producing oscillating corrections to scaling, and a correlation-length exponent ν=2/a at the new fixed point. The authors argue that this scaling relation is exact and more general than their specific model. They state that the criterion applies to long-range-correlated percolation and that triangular-Ising percolation results agree with the predictions.
limitations: The full paper was not readable in this verification, so its derivations, precise parameter regimes, detailed assumptions, and any caveats in the body cannot be assessed here. The publisher abstract characterizes the m-vector analysis as an ε- and δ-expansion and presents exactness of ν=2/a as the authors’ argument; the abstract alone does not permit independent evaluation of that claim. No supplement was found linked from the publisher record, but its absence cannot be established conclusively from the sources available.
relationship_to_projects: For a spatial percolation manuscript, this is directly relevant background if the manuscript studies quenched, spatially long-range-correlated site or bond occupation: the paper explicitly applies its extended Harris criterion to that setting. It is not by itself evidence for a particular numerical implementation or for percolation with uncorrelated disorder. For a one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, there is no direct model or method match in the abstract: it concerns critical phenomena, quenched disorder, and percolation rather than a one-orbital interface Hamiltonian. It could be conceptual background only if that notebook explicitly models spatially correlated quenched disorder and critical scaling; otherwise relevance is weak.
full_text_status: The APS publisher record and abstract were accessible. The APS PDF endpoint and its alternate link were blocked by a CAPTCHA/access controls, and the publisher harvest endpoint did not yield readable full text. OpenAlex lists the work as closed access with no repository full-text location. I therefore verified and read the abstract, not the full article or an accepted manuscript. No supplement is linked or indicated on the consulted APS record; I cannot rule out an unindexed supplement.
evidence_stance: The candidate is verified as an existing paper with the stated exact title, authors, Physical Review B venue, year, page range, and DOI. Bibliographic details are supported by the APS DOI/publisher record, Crossref, and INSPIRE-HEP. Scientific-content statements above are explicitly limited to what the APS abstract reports; the full text and any supplement were not inspected, so no claim is made to have independently validated its derivations.

citation: K. J. Schrenk, N. Posé, J. J. Kranz, L. V. M. van Kessenich, N. A. M. Araújo, and H. J. Herrmann, “Percolation with long-range correlated disorder,” Physical Review E 88, 052102 (2013), published November 4, 2013.
research_question: How do long-range power-law spatial correlations in site-occupation disorder affect two-dimensional percolation thresholds, critical exponents, cluster geometry, transport, and bridge-site growth as a function of the Hurst exponent H?
methods_and_model: Monte Carlo finite-size study of site percolation on triangular-lattice stripes, using ranked random-height landscapes: sites are occupied in order of their height, producing the desired occupied fraction p. Long-range-correlated heights are generated with the Fourier filtering method. The authors use cluster labeling/Newman–Ziff methods and analyze finite-size scaling of the percolation threshold, largest cluster and cluster-size second moment, perimeters, shortest paths, backbone and red sites, conductivity (by solving Kirchhoff equations on the backbone), and bridge sites. The paper also uses perimeter yardstick estimates and scaling collapses for selected observables.
main_findings: The triangular-lattice threshold is argued and numerically checked to be pc=1/2 for the correlated model considered. The correlation-length scaling is compatible with nu_H=-1/H in the correlated regime, while uncorrelated exponents persist below the extended-Harris crossover. For H approaching zero, the largest-cluster fractal dimension and gamma_H/nu_H increase; the complete and accessible perimeter dimensions approach 3/2; the backbone becomes more compact, shortest-path dimension decreases toward 1, and the reduced conductivity exponent decreases. Bridge-site growth behaves differently above the correlation crossover; for example, the reported bridge-growth exponent at H=-0.85 is 0.64±0.06. The authors propose simple functional fits for several exponent dependencies on H.
limitations: Scope is a particular two-dimensional correlated site-percolation construction on triangular-lattice stripes, with Fourier-filtered height disorder and H in [-1,0]; conclusions should not be transferred unchanged to other dimensions, lattices, disorder-generation schemes, or observables. Several exponent formulas are empirical proposals based on finite-size numerical data. The authors report increasingly severe finite-size effects as H approaches zero for red-site scaling. For bridge growth in the correlated regime, the uncorrelated-style size collapse does not hold, and the manuscript does not claim a single corresponding crossover law there. No separate supplemental document was found in the inspected publisher/arXiv records.
relationship_to_projects: Spatial percolation manuscript: directly relevant background if that manuscript studies two-dimensional correlated site percolation, cluster geometry, transport, or Hurst-exponent-dependent finite-size scaling. It can support comparison and motivate tests, but its model-specific threshold and fitted exponent laws require matching assumptions before application. One-orbital interface tight-binding notebook: only tangential background on disorder/percolation concepts; the paper does not study electronic tight-binding Hamiltonians, orbitals, interfaces, or electronic transport, so it does not directly validate that notebook’s model or results.
full_text_status: The APS publisher record and abstract were accessible, but APS full text was subscription/authorization gated. The full author manuscript was accessible and inspected on arXiv (HTML v2 and linked PDF). No separate supplement was listed on the APS or arXiv record inspected.
evidence_stance: Verified exact record. APS publisher metadata and PubMed independently agree on title, author list, journal, volume/article number, year, and DOI; arXiv identifies the same journal reference and supplies an accessible full author manuscript. The candidate’s citation fields are correct. Full publisher article access was unavailable, so content findings are based on the complete accessible arXiv manuscript rather than a subscription copy; the publisher abstract was also read.

citation: Johannes Zierenberg, Niklas Fricke, Martin Marenz, F. P. Spitzner, Viktoria Blavatska, and Wolfhard Janke, "Percolation thresholds and fractal dimensions for square and cubic lattices with long-range correlated defects," Physical Review E 96, 062125 (2017), published 18 December 2017.
research_question: How do long-range power-law-correlated site defects affect percolation thresholds and the fractal dimension of critical largest clusters on square (2D) and cubic (3D) lattices? The authors also test sensitivity to the metric used to define correlation distances and whether changes in fractal dimension follow the extended Harris criterion.
methods_and_model: Numerical site percolation on periodic square and cubic lattices. Gaussian continuous site variables with covariance generated using a discrete Fourier-filtering method were thresholded into occupied/defect sites. The target covariance was C(r)=(1+r²)^(-a/2), with both Euclidean and Manhattan distance metrics tested. A global (ensemble-level) occupation-density mapping was used. A cluster was considered percolating when it wrapped across a specified lattice boundary. Threshold estimates came from finite-size extrapolation; cluster fractal dimensions were obtained by fitting the largest-cluster mass against lattice size. They generated 10^5 replicas per size: L=64–8192 in 2D and L=8–512 in 3D.
main_findings: Percolation thresholds depend strongly on details of the correlation function and metric, whereas the largest-cluster fractal dimension is reported to be metric-independent within their numerical precision. Correlations generally lower the threshold. Examples from their tables: in 2D at a=0.5, p_c=0.5239(3) for Euclidean distance and 0.5054(3) for Manhattan distance; in 3D at a=0.5 the estimates are 0.025(3) and 0.030(2), respectively. For weak correlations the fractal dimension returns to the uncorrelated value (91/48 in 2D; about 2.52295 in 3D). In 2D it rises as correlations strengthen, e.g. d_f=1.9128(5) at a=0.5 and 1.9602(8) at a=0.1, tending toward 2. The onset of the 2D change is not set simply by the extended Harris threshold. In 3D, estimates remain near the uncorrelated value for a≥1.5, but strong-correlation fits are unreliable at a≤1.
limitations: The authors explicitly emphasize that p_c is nonuniversal and quantitatively dependent on short-range model details, including the metric and correlation-generation implementation. Their finite-size scaling ansatz for 3D thresholds is empirically motivated; strong correlations produce non-self-averaging/segregation effects, and the a=0.5 and 1 threshold estimates warrant caution. The 3D fractal-dimension fits do not work convincingly for a≤1, and the authors attribute some apparent behavior near the Harris crossover to unmodeled corrections to scaling. Their results are for lattice site percolation, not a general continuum, bond-percolation, or electronic-transport model.
relationship_to_projects: For a spatial percolation manuscript, this is a directly relevant benchmark if the manuscript treats lattice site percolation with power-law-correlated disorder: it supplies explicit square/cubic threshold estimates, fractal dimensions, and a clear warning that thresholds depend on metric and disorder construction. Comparisons should match the authors' global threshold mapping, periodic boundaries, wrapping definition, correlation function, and dimensionality; it is not a universal numeric benchmark outside that setup. For the one-orbital interface tight-binding notebook, relevance is only conceptual and indirect: the paper concerns classical geometric connectivity of occupied lattice sites, not a tight-binding Hamiltonian, interface states, orbital physics, conductance, or electronic localization, so it cannot validate those notebook results or provide direct numerical parameters.
full_text_status: The APS publisher record was accessible for bibliographic metadata and abstract, but the full publisher article required authorization. The complete accepted manuscript was accessible as arXiv:1708.02296v2 (HTML, 2 January 2018) and inspected, including its three appendices. No separately linked supplement was found on the APS or arXiv records; the paper's appendices are part of the manuscript.
evidence_stance: Verified exact existence and the supplied title, six authors, journal, volume/article number, publication year, and DOI against the APS publisher record; PubMed independently agrees, and arXiv links the manuscript to the same journal citation and DOI. Research details above are based on the accessible full arXiv manuscript rather than abstract-only inference. Publisher full text was not accessible, and no separate supplement was located.

citation: Yueying Li, Wenjie Sun, Jiangfeng Yang, Xiangbin Cai, Wei Guo, Zhengbin Gu, Ye Zhu, and Yuefeng Nie, “Impact of Cation Stoichiometry on the Crystalline Structure and Superconductivity in Nickelates,” Frontiers in Physics 9, article 719534 (2021).
research_question: How nominal cation stoichiometry in MBE-grown NdNiO3 and Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO3 precursor films affects structure, reduction, and superconducting transport, and whether out-of-plane lattice parameter can guide flux calibration.
methods_and_model: Full open-access publisher article read. NdNiO3 and Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO3 films were grown by MBE on TiO2-terminated SrTiO3 while varying nominal Nd:Ni flux. RHEED, QCM, XRD/RSM, AFM, STEM/ADF, and four-probe transport were used. Reduction used CaH2 at 280 C for 4 h.
main_findings: Off-optimal nominal Nd:Ni ratios associate with expanded out-of-plane lattice parameter; the authors fit this relation to guide MBE flux adjustment. Nominally 10% off-stoichiometric films show broader/weaker precursor peaks and some reduced-phase peaks; at 15% deviation few obvious infinite-layer peaks are observed. Off-stoichiometric reduced samples are insulating; the optimized sample has onset about 14.7 K and zero resistance about 4.7 K. RHEED impurity features are unresolved.
limitations: The composition is a nominal beam-flux ratio, not direct absolute cation assay. Anion concentration also affects the lattice parameter. Diffraction and transport do not establish a general chemical endpoint. The study does not validate a cross-facility/batch predictor and reports no magnetic measurement.
relationship_to_projects: Supports a narrow precursor-composition/structure relation and process-specific calibration. It does not establish an independent-batch predictor, definitive reduction endpoint, or magnetic response.
full_text_status: Full open-access publisher HTML read; arXiv record checked; PDF not separately read.
evidence_stance: Exact journal citation verified; support is narrow and process-specific.

citation: A. Gutiérrez-Llorente, A. Raji, D. Zhang, L. Divay, A. Gloter, F. Gallego, C. Galindo, M. Bibes, and L. Iglesias, “Toward Reliable Synthesis of Superconducting Infinite Layer Nickelate Thin Films by Topochemical Reduction,” Advanced Science 11(24), article 2309092 (2024).
research_question: How precursor film quality and progressive CaH2 topochemical reduction affect superconducting transport in Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO2 thin films, including whether transport can track reduction progress.
methods_and_model: Full article read via PMC and arXiv v2. 10–13-unit-cell Pr0.8Sr0.2NiO3 films were grown by PLD on STO; XPS assessed cation stoichiometry. A 5×5 mm film was cut into pieces; one piece was repeatedly reduced in evacuated sealed ampoules at 260 C for successive 150, 30, 25, and 45 min steps. XRD/RSM, four-probe transport, STEM/4D-STEM were used.
main_findings: A resistive transition appeared after initial reduction; zero resistance followed further reduction. The final series reached onset near 9 K and Tc about 7.6 K. Structural data support the infinite-layer phase and apical-oxygen removal. Over-reduction can lower onset and deteriorate films.
limitations: The central reduction trajectory is repeated treatment of the same specimen/piece, not independent batch replication; no success-rate or yield analysis. The system is ultrathin Pr0.8Sr0.2 on STO and one sealed-ampoule protocol. The accessible paper does not report magnetic screening; the supplementary PDF was not inspected.
relationship_to_projects: Supports treatment progression and transport sensitivity for this specific Pr platform, but not independent-batch reproducibility or a general endpoint criterion. It does not validate spatial percolation or a nickelate interface Hamiltonian.
full_text_status: Publisher metadata plus full PMC and arXiv v2 article text read; supplement PDF could not be retrieved.
evidence_stance: Exact published citation verified. The preprint title uses “Towards”; published title uses “Toward.”

citation: Damjan Pelc, Marija Vučković, Mihael S. Grbić, Miroslav Požek, Guichuan Yu, Takao Sasagawa, Martin Greven, and Neven Barišić, “Emergence of superconductivity in the cuprates via a universal percolation process,” Nature Communications 9, 4327 (2018).
research_question: Can superconducting precursor signals above Tc in several cuprates be explained by spatially inhomogeneous superconducting patches whose macroscopic response emerges by percolation?
methods_and_model: Experimental nonlinear conductivity in multiple cuprate families plus a minimal nearest-neighbour site-percolation model of square/cubic patches. Local superconducting fraction P(T) is related to temperature; the simple model uses Pπ−P=(T−Tπ)/Ξ0 and explores a distribution of local gaps. Patches are static; Josephson couplings and proximity effects are neglected.
main_findings: The measured nonlinear conductivity decays with temperature and field on a scale Ξ0. A minimal inhomogeneous-percolation model captures the reported dependencies better than the tested standard GL treatment. The paper reports site thresholds near 0.6 for 2D and 0.3 for 3D in its chosen lattice models.
limitations: The model assumes static, perfectly connected patches and omits Josephson/proximity effects; the authors note these assumptions are poor in regimes near Tc or well above it. The reported evidence is for cuprates, not nickelates, and does not validate a reduction-proxy window or correlated random field for nickelate films.
relationship_to_projects: Directly shows that the general idea “local superconducting patches become globally superconducting by percolation” is established in cuprate literature. The nickelate manuscript must claim a narrower contribution: a material-calibrated proxy, covariance-controlled prediction, or batch-level validation—not generic percolative emergence.
full_text_status: Full open-access PMC article read; supplementary information is listed and available, but not separately inspected in this targeted review.
evidence_stance: Peer-reviewed experimental/model paper; relevant prior art, not direct nickelate evidence.

citation: Han-Byul Jang, Ji Soo Lim, and Chan-Ho Yang, “Film-thickness-driven superconductor to insulator transition in cuprate superconductors,” Scientific Reports 10, article 3236 (2020).
research_question: How film thickness affects the superconductor-insulator transition in optimally doped La1.85Sr0.15CuO4 epitaxial films.
methods_and_model: Full open article read. PLD LSCO films on lattice-matched LaAlO3 ranged from 6 to about 300 nm. Four-probe transport, XRD/RSM, STEM, and XPS were used. The paper interprets thickness-dependent transport using disorder, oxygen vacancies, weak localization, and a percolation picture; it is not a direct spatially resolved percolation simulation.
main_findings: Transport shows a thickness-driven transition near 10 nm. XPS suggests oxygen vacancies near the interface. The authors discuss local superconducting and metallic/insulating states and state that supercurrent paths must percolate; the effective dimensionality and percolation threshold may depend on film thickness and coherence length.
limitations: The percolation mechanism is proposed rather than directly mapped or measured. Data availability is by reasonable request. LSCO results cannot be transferred quantitatively to nickelates.
relationship_to_projects: Demonstrates prior discussion of thickness, disorder, oxygen vacancies, and percolation in superconducting oxide films. It narrows the novelty of generic “correlation changes connectivity” while reinforcing the need for spatially resolved validation.
full_text_status: Full open Nature/Springer article read, including methods, discussion, conclusion, and data statement.
evidence_stance: Peer-reviewed experimental evidence with a proposed, not directly verified, percolative interpretation.

citation: K. H. Sarwa B. Tan, Kevin A. Parendo, and A. M. Goldman, “Evidence of spatially inhomogeneous pairing on the insulating side of a disorder-tuned superconductor-insulator transition,” Physical Review B 78, 014506 (2008).
research_question: Whether insulating amorphous InxOy films near a disorder-tuned superconducting transition contain spatially inhomogeneous superconducting pairing even without granular morphology.
methods_and_model: Transport, magnetic-field dependence, and nonlinear conductance-voltage measurements on amorphous InxOy films; films were annealed at low temperature to tune resistance. A network/percolation interpretation treats superconducting clusters as Josephson-coupled islands in an insulating matrix, with global zero-resistance behavior requiring a spanning supercluster.
main_findings: The authors observe strong resistance upturns and nonlinear conductance consistent with local pairing islands on the insulating side. They argue that islands or superclusters do not form a film-spanning superconducting path in this regime.
limitations: The evidence is indirect transport/tunneling-like behavior, not a spatial image of pairing domains. The percolation network is conceptual and does not establish nickelate oxygen-proxy thresholds. Publisher full text is gated; full arXiv manuscript was read.
relationship_to_projects: Directly establishes prior physical discussion of local superconducting islands and percolating global paths in disordered films. It cautions against equating a geometric threshold map with a measured transport path without coupling and conductance physics.
full_text_status: Full arXiv manuscript v2 read; APS publisher record and abstract checked; publisher article text required authorization.
evidence_stance: Peer-reviewed paper with full accessible author manuscript; interpretation is based on transport evidence.

citation: I. Tamir et al., “Sensitivity of the superconducting state in thin films,” Science Advances 5(3), eaau3826 (2019).
research_question: Whether the low-temperature metallic-like transport observed in thin superconductors is intrinsic or can be induced by external measurement perturbations.
methods_and_model: Full PMC article read. Compared amorphous indium-oxide and exfoliated 2H-NbSe2 films, used external low-pass filtering, varied measurement current, and measured resistance versus temperature and magnetic field.
main_findings: Filtering electrical lines removed apparent low-temperature resistance saturation in the studied cases; higher measurement current could reintroduce saturation. The paper attributes these effects to sensitivity/heating, emphasizing careful filtering and low-current checks.
limitations: The study does not model percolation and concerns different superconductors; it is a measurement-control precedent, not nickelate-specific evidence. Its conclusions should not be generalized beyond the tested samples without qualification.
relationship_to_projects: Relevant to the proposed joint transport-plus-magnetic endpoint: it underscores that current, filtering, and thermalization controls matter before assigning connectivity or superconducting mechanisms from transport alone.
